claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a random BCC solid solution.
Atomic size mismatch and chemical disorder cause severe local lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal annealing or controlled cooling can induce chemical short-range order in the alloy.
The induced short-range order consists specifically of ordered B2-like HfTi and TiZr clusters.
Ordered B2-like regions can form while a disordered BCC matrix is retained.
There is a temperature window below the order-disorder transition and above the onset of dominant macroscopic phase separation in which SRO clusters percolate without becoming precipitates.
HfTi and TiZr B2-like clusters act as local strain-relief zones.
Formation of the ordered clusters reduces RMS atomic displacement amplitudes relative to the random alloy.
The ordered clusters form a connected percolative network that supports coherent phonon transport.
Transition from random chemical occupancy to B2-like ordering reduces local chemical-strain lattice distortion.
Reduced local lattice distortion lowers the scattering cross-section for high-frequency phonons.
Percolating ordered clusters create low-resistance pathways for phonon propagation.
The reduction in disorder scattering and the percolative pathways outweigh scattering at cluster-matrix interfaces.
Percolative B2-like ordering increases the mean free path and group velocity of high-frequency phonons.
The SRO-percolative state has higher lattice thermal conductivity than the random solid solution.
The conductivity increase is accompanied by narrower high-frequency phonon DOS peaks.
The conductivity increase is accompanied by lower Debye-Waller factors for the cluster-forming elements.
Below the cluster percolation threshold, isolated ordered clusters behave primarily as phonon-scattering centers and decrease conductivity.
Above the percolation threshold, connected ordered clusters behave as transport pathways and increase conductivity.
Macroscopic phase separation or long-range ordering introduces enough interfacial scattering to reverse the conductivity increase.
